newsitem.title: USA: Weak Japanese data, Euro woes propel dollar.
newsitem.headline: Weak Japanese data, Euro woes propel dollar.

text.p: The dollar rallied against major currencies Friday on new signs of economic weakness in Japan and further worries about Europe's planned single currency.
The dollar hit a 10-day high against the German mark and came within a whisker of its 1997 high.
It also rose against the Japanese yen after Japan said industrial output rose 3.8 percent in May but projected a decline in June and reported its highest unemployment rate in 44 years.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita defended Japan's low interest rates, saying they could not rise until the economy strengthened. Higher Japanese rates would boost the yen by making Japanese assets more attractive to investors.

"The negative economic news means Japan may not be raising interest rates as soon as people thought and that caused the dollar to climb," said Thomas Arnold, chief foreign exchange dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank.

The economy in the United States has been strong by contrast. The University of Michigan's June consumer sentiment index hit a record, people who saw the report said Friday, and the government revised first quarter growth to a 5.9 percent rate, up from 5.8 percent in its previous estimate.
The dollar rose to 114.58 yen late in New York from 113.15 late on Thursday.

Meanwhile, European officials continued to predict key nations would fail to cut their budget deficits to 3 percent of gross domestic product, the benchmark for joining the planned currency, the euro.
That boosted the dollar against European currencies, including the mark. The dollar jumped to 1.7385 marks from 1.7255 late on Thursday.
The British pound, which rose to a six-year high against the mark, fell to $1.6647 from $1.6657. The dollar also rose to 1.4525 Swiss francs from 1.4360. It fell to Canadian $1.3803 from C$1.3821.
"Most people still believe monetary union will take place, but the uncertainties surrounding it gave the dollar a boost," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

A French government source was quoted as saying France would only get down to 3.5 percent in 1997 and Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen noted that Germany seemed unable and France unwilling to meet the requirements.

Many experts now see a less stringent application of the euro criteria, which could lead to a wider group of countries taking part, including traditionally weaker currencies like the Italian lira and the Spanish peseta.
That would tend to weaken the mark and strengthen the dollar, traders said.
"There's a lot of pressure on the mark across the board. That's also propelling the dollar," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer.
The mark also fell against the pound, which will not join the euro group, and the lira, despite an Italian interest rate cut.
